title: Mara and the Contact
premise: Odile Voss, a hostage negotiator haunted by the one call she failed — a young man named Tomas who died mid-negotiation eight years ago — receives calls from his voice on a burner phone that shouldn't exist. The voice leads her to discover that Tomas was an asset of Meridian, a private 'crisis resolution' firm that trains negotiators through live hostage scenarios, some staged, some not, and silences those who learn too much. As Odile infiltrates Meridian posing as a recruit, she uncovers that her own celebrated career was quietly engineered by them, and that the man who trained her, Aldous Crane, intends to use her as the fall figure in a political kidnapping gone wrong. In the end she turns Meridian's own negotiation protocols against Crane in a final phone standoff, burns the network's records publicly at the cost of her reputation, and chooses survival over vindication — walking away with the truth instead of the credit.
about_author: Orsen Ravensworth is the pen name of a former crisis-line volunteer who spent six years listening to strangers talk each other back from ledges before turning to fiction. He writes thrillers about people whose professional calm is a mask over unpayable debts.

chapters.title: The Go-Bag
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. We meet her mid-negotiation, talking a bank robber down with flawless technique, then home to her apartment: packed bag, sleeping pills, a framed photo of a negotiation class she keeps face-down. Establishes her polished lie — that the Tomas case closed clean. Emotional beat: competence as armor.

chapters.title: A Voice Eight Years Dead
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. A burner phone arrives in her mail slot; when it rings, the voice is unmistakably Tomas, reciting details only he could know — including the last thing he said to her before the line went dead. He tells her to look up the address of a warehouse fire she never connected to him. Emotional beat: dread dressed as hope.

chapters.title: Warehouse Nine
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, with a brief interlude from Detective Ilsa Brandt, who once suspected Odile in the Tomas case. At the burned warehouse Odile finds training debris: role-play scripts, restraint gear, a roster with Tomas's name redacted — and hers listed under 'graduates.' Emotional beat: the floor giving way beneath her own history.

chapters.title: Meridian
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Following the roster, she approaches Meridian Solutions, a glossy consultancy for 'high-stakes communication,' and talks her way into an assessment interview. She recognizes their methods as her own methods — taught to her by mentor Aldous Crane. Crane greets her warmly, too warmly. Emotional beat: flattery with teeth.

chapters.title: The Curriculum
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Odile inside Meridian's assessment weekend, and chapters of Tomas's recovered journal read in his voice. His entries reveal trainees were tested against real hostages, real stakes, and failures were 'retired.' Odile realizes her famous success rate was curated — she was never tested against anything Meridian didn't control. Emotional beat: grief curdling into rage.

chapters.title: Live Exercise
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Mid-assessment, a 'training scenario' goes live: a genuine kidnapping of a junior minister, run by Meridian as both job and demonstration. Odile is ordered to negotiate — and realizes the kidnappers are taking cues from someone feeding them her playbook. Emotional beat: performing perfectly while understanding it's a trap.

chapters.title: What Crane Built
chapters.summary: Crane's POV, first time. His chapter reveals the design: Meridian manufactures crises to sell resolutions to governments, and Odile is meant to be the public face when this one breaks badly — the negotiator whose 'failure' justifies privatizing all crisis response. He genuinely believes he made her. Emotional beat: corruption convinced it's craftsmanship.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The burner rings again: Tomas's voice explains he recorded everything before his death, and the recordings are hidden where she must trade herself to get them. Brandt, now suspicious of Meridian, offers uneasy alliance. Odile surrenders her badge and walks into Meridian's hands deliberately. Emotional beat: choosing the fall on her own terms.

chapters.title: Held
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, captive in Meridian's facility. Crane stages a final 'negotiation' — her life traded for the recordings' location, broadcast internally as a training exercise. Instead she negotiates the room itself: turning two technicians, exposing the dead-man's switch on the recordings, forcing Crane to choose between killing her on tape and losing everything. Emotional beat: every skill she owns, spent at once.

chapters.title: Signal Lost
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, closing with Brandt's epilogue frame. The recordings go public; Meridian collapses; Crane takes the exit he always taught — but Odile declines credit, letting the story attribute the leak to a dead man. Final scene: she unpacks the go-bag at last, keeps one burner phone, and answers a stranger's crisis line as a volunteer. Emotional beat: survival without absolution, chosen anyway.
